meta.title: Bengali B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1,000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Bengali → English (see the Bengali, recall the meaning) and English → Bengali (see an English meaning, recall the Bengali). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1,000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences, events, dreams, hopes and ambitions and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for learners of Bengali, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 297 of the 1,000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and careers, education and learning, the news, the media and the arts, computers and the internet, nature, the weather and the environment, society, politics and the law, money and services, health and lifestyle, travel and getting about, feelings and relationships, ideas, opinions and reasons, the words that connect an argument, describing, and the verbs of doing, including the common multi-word verbs — and the other 703 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Bengali, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The deck teaches the standard colloquial language (cholito bhasha) shared by West Bengal and Bangladesh; where an everyday word differs between the two — জল and পানি for water, নমস্কার and সালাম for a greeting — both are taught. Every headword is printed in the Bengali script with a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (ô for the open o of the inherent vowel, ō where the o-sign is written, a dot under the retroflex letters, ẏ and ẇ for the glides: kôra, bhalō), so the deck can be studied before the script is fluent; the Bengali Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script itself. Bengali has no grammatical gender. The 696 nouns show their definite form ('the …', with -টা), their plural and their genitive ('of …'); the 67 verbs show their present, their past and their 'having done' form, where the stem's vowel changes and the irregular verbs show, and behind the All forms fold every tense by person, at the three levels of address — তুই intimate, তুমি familiar, আপনি polite. Real example sentences come with 370 of the 1,000 words, three apiece for 96 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
